4793               	;
4794               	; 	' 8-3-8 IS EDGE-TRIGGERED AND ANY STRAY DIGIT RESETS IT (see title_wait).
4795               	; 	'
4796               	; 	' It used to read cont1.key raw every pass and test only for the digit it
4797               	; 	' wanted next. That worked -- but only because 8-3-8 ALTERNATES, so holding
4798               	; 	' 8 cannot advance past the first step. It is an accident of the sequence
4799               	; 	' rather than a design, and it had two costs: 8,5,3,9,8 opened this page as
4800               	; 	' readily as 8,3,8, and a key that READS as held for many frames got a free
4801               	; 	' walk through the state machine.
4802               	; 	'
4803               	; 	' That second one is not hypothetical on this machine. ALPHA LOCK shorts a
4804               	; 	' keyboard line -- and Classic99 defaults to invertcaps, so it reads DOWN
4805               	; 	' with the host's Caps Lock UP -- and this page was reached twice from
4806               	; 	' single keypresses while testing an unrelated change.
4807               	; 	'
4808               	; 	' The reset is the DEFAULT rather than a test for a particular wrong digit:
4809               	; 	' Bust-A-Bobble resets only on a stray 3 and still lets 8,5,3,8 through.
4810               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------------- 838 setup page

5518               	;
5519               	; 	' ======================================================================
5520               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
5521               	; 	' ======================================================================
5522               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
5523               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
5524               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
5525               	; 	' of running.
5526               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
5527               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
5528               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
5529               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
5530               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
5531               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
5532               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
5533               	; 	'
5534               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
5535               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
5536               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
5537               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
5538               	; 	'
5539               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
5540               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
5541               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
5542               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
5543               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
5544               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
5545               	; 	'
5546               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
5547               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
5548               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
5549               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
5550               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
5551               	; 	'
5552               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
5553               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
5554               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).
5555               	; draw_screen:
5556               cvb_DRAW_SCREEN
5557               	; 	#if NES

5561               	; 	'
5562               	; 	' A DARK BLUE BACKDROP WAS TRIED HERE, to give the sunset a fourth band

5564               	; 	' escalator, the radar ground and every black outline in the store, all of

5628               	; 		#ddst = #ddst + 96		' three rows down -- see the overscan note
5629               	; 		' ONE ROW A FRAME, AND THIS IS WHY THREE BANDS IN FOUR LOST THEIR
5630               	; 		' LAST TWO ROWS. The NMI copies PPUBUF into the PPU during vblank
5631               	; 		' and its copy loop DOES NOT STOP WHEN VBLANK ENDS -- it runs to
5632               	; 		' the end of the descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and a
5633               	; 		' PPUDATA write outside vblank is discarded by the hardware.
5634               	; 		'
5635               	; 		' NTSC gives about 2273 CPU cycles of vblank, OAM DMA takes 513 of
5636               	; 		' them, and the copy costs roughly 14 a byte: about a hundred bytes
5637               	; 		' get through. A 32x5 band is 160, so the last sixty-odd vanished
5638               	; 		' -- three whole rows arrived, the fourth stopped eight or nine
5639               	; 		' cells in, and the floor bar and the air row above it were simply
5640               	; 		' never there. Measured on screen as `#########.......`, on every
5641               	; 		' band whose blit did not happen to start early.
5642               	; 		'
5643               	; 		' A row is 32 bytes, which fits with room to spare. This costs four
5644               	; 		' extra frames per band at round start and nothing during play.

5703               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5704               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top
5705               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5706               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5707               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5708               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5709               	; 	'
5710               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5711               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5712               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5713               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5714               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5715               	; 	'

5717               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band

6344               	; 			' PER KIND, not one global speed (see start_krook).
6345               	; 			' THE SPEED IS A PROPERTY OF THE KIND, and obs() only ever
6346               	; 			' held a copy of it -- set from the kind here, zeroed for a
6347               	; 			' radio below, and read in one place. upd_obst derives it
6348               	; 			' from obk() instead, which is 8 bytes of RAM back and one
6349               	; 			' fewer thing that can disagree with itself.
6350               	; 			' THEY COME FROM THE FAR SIDE. Kelly walked into this screen
6351               	; 			' from one edge, so the obstacles start at the OTHER edge and
6352               	; 			' run toward him. Crossing a seam then always presents an
6353               	; 			' ONCOMING stream, never a set of backs he has to catch up
6354               	; 			' with -- and it means the direction he is travelling is
6355               	; 			' always the direction the danger comes from.
6356               	; 			'
6357               	; 			' The table's x becomes a stagger from that edge rather than
6358               	; 			' an absolute position, and the slot index spreads them out
6359               	; 			' so they arrive in sequence instead of as one wall.
6360               	; 			'
6361               	; 			' THE SECOND ONE IS A FIXED DISTANCE BEHIND THE FIRST, AND
6362               	; 			' THAT DISTANCE IS SET BY THE JUMP.
6363               	; 			'
6364               	; 			' It used to be `(lx AND 63) + 64` -- a masked byte out of
6365               	; 			' the placement table plus a constant -- so the gap between
6366               	; 			' the two hazards was whatever those two bytes happened to
6367               	; 			' differ by. Measured across the five populated screens it
6368               	; 			' came out 46, 46, 70, 70, 70 px. Screens 2 and 4 flank the
6369               	; 			' elevator, so the store had a visibly tighter pair on one
6370               	; 			' side of it than the other, which is exactly how it was
6371               	; 			' reported from play.
6372               	; 			'
6373               	; 			' Both numbers are too small, which is the real fault. Kelly
6374               	; 			' closes on an oncoming hazard at (KWALK64 + its speed)/64
6375               	; 			' px a FRAME, and the jump is airborne 28 frames, so a jump
6376               	; 			' eats 82 px of closing distance at the fastest hazard. At
6377               	; 			' 46 or 70 there is NO screen where he can land between the
6378               	; 			' two: he clears the first and comes down on the second.
6379               	; 			'

6494               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6495               	; 			'
6496               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6497               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6498               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6499               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6500               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6501               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6502               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
6503               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
6504               	; 			'
6505               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6506               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6507               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6508               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6509               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6510               	; 			'
6511               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
6512               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6513               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
6514               	; 			'
6515               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
6516               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
6517               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
6518               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
6519               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after

8055               	; 		' him a few pixels and made NO sound at all. That does not read as
8056               	; 		' a short step, it reads as the controls being ignored, and it is
8057               	; 		' worst exactly where a player taps rather than holds: lining up a
8058               	; 		' jump, or edging around a hazard.

8991               	;
8992               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
8993               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
8994               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
8995               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
8996               	; 	'
8997               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
8998               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
8999               	; 	'
9000               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
9001               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
9002               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
9003               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
9004               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
9005               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
9006               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
9007               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
9008               	; 	' merged object.
9009               	; 	'
9010               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
9011               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
9012               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
9013               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
9014               	; 	'
9015               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
9016               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
9017               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
9018               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
9019               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
9020               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
9021               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
9022               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
9023               	; 	'
9024               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
9025               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
9026               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
9027               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
9028               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
9029               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
9030               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
9031               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
9032               	; 	' its bottom half together.
9033               	; 	'
9034               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
9035               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
9036               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
9037               	; 	#if NES
9038               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
9039               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
9040               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
9041               	; 	'
9042               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
9043               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
9044               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
9045               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
9046               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
9047               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
9048               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
9049               	; 	'
9050               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
9051               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
9052               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
9053               	; 	'
9054               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
9055               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
9056               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
9057               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
9058               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
9059               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
9060               	; 	'                   the whole time.
9061               	; 	'
9062               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
9063               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
9064               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
9065               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
9066               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
9067               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
9068               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
9069               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
9070               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
9071               	; 	'
9072               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
9073               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
9074               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
9075               	; 	' they only need setting once.
9076               	; 	'
9077               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
9078               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
9079               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
9080               	; 	' as him changing pose.
9081               	; nes_swp16:
9082               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
9083               	; 	'
9084               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
9085               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
9086               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
9087               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
9088               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
9089               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
9090               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
9091               	; 	'
9092               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
9093               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
9094               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
9095               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
9096               	; 	'
9097               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
9098               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
9099               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
9100               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
9101               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
9102               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0
9103               	; 	SPRITE 5,SPRHID,0,0,0
9104               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0
9105               	; 	SPRITE 7,SPRHID,0,0,0
9106               	; 	ASM JSR nes_oam2
9107               	; 	nchr = P_HSTB
9108               	; 	ntab = 0
9109               	; 	#ncol = 0
9110               	; 	nink = 1
9111               	; 	ncnt = 4
9112               	; 	WAIT
9113               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9114               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32		' four patterns of source art, 8 bytes each
9115               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
9116               	; 	WAIT
9117               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9118               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
9119               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
9120               	; 	WAIT
9121               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9122               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
9123               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
9124               	; 	WAIT
9125               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9126               	; 	RETURN
9127               	;
9128               	; nes_def:
9129               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
9130               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
9131               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
9132               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
9133               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
9134               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
9135               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
9136               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
9137               	; 	RETURN
9138               	;
9139               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
9140               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
9141               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
9142               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
9143               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
9144               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.
9145               	; 	'
9146               	; 	' THE NAME IS HISTORICAL: it was written for esc_tick, which redefines six
9147               	; 	' characters EVERY PASS on the two escalator screens and ran visibly slow
9148               	; 	' on nes_def. Nothing about it is escalator-specific -- it takes the same
9149               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
9150               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
9151               	; 	' flashing title screen.
9152               	; 	'
9153               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
9154               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.
9155               	; nes_escd:
9156               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrq
9157               	; 	RETURN
9158               	;
9159               	; nes_tpl:
9160               	; 	nti = lv8(nbl)
9161               	; 	nti = nti + klsc

9251               	;
9252               	; 	' A PILLAR'S CAP MAY BE CLEARED; AN END WALL'S MAY NOT. beam_one stamps
9253               	; 	' both into the slab row of the band above, but they mean different
9254               	; 	' things. SLABP is the top of a free-standing pillar: a radio or a prize
9255               	; 	' stands in front of the pillar, so leaving its cap up there hangs a grey
9256               	; 	' stub over the fixture and that is what this routine exists to remove.
9257               	; 	' SLABE and ROOFSE are written ONLY at column 0 and column 31 -- read
9258               	; 	' beam_one, they are the two edge cases -- and there they are the
9259               	; 	' BUILDING'S OUTSIDE WALL, carrying its brick bond up through the floor
9260               	; 	' above. Clearing those took the support out from under the storey above
9261               	; 	' at the very edge of the screen, so the second floor visibly rested on
9262               	; 	' nothing.
9263               	; 	'
9264               	; 	' It could only ever show on the ESCALATOR screens, which is exactly how
9265               	; 	' it was reported -- one side, then mirrored on the other. The flight
9266               	; 	' fills the middle of an escalator band, so that screen's radio or prize
9267               	; 	' is pushed right out against the end wall; on every other screen no
9268               	; 	' fixture sits close enough for the two-cell clear at #bca and #bca+1 to
9269               	; 	' reach column 0 or 31.
9270               	; beam_clear:
9271               cvb_BEAM_CLEAR
9272               	; 	' A BEAM TOP IS NOT IN THE TEMPLATE. beam_one VPOKEs it into the row
9273               	; 	' ABOVE each band, out of the pillar-column table -- so on the NES this
9274               	; 	' asks that same table rather than the PPU, and #bca sits one row above
9275               	; 	' the band, which is why it cannot go through nes_tpl.
9276               	; 	'
9277               	; 	' IT ALSO REPRODUCES beam_one'S EXCLUSION OF COLUMNS 0 AND 31. Those
9278               	; 	' carry SLABE/ROOFSE, the building's OUTSIDE WALL, not a pillar cap --
9279               	; 	' and clearing structure because an erase routine could not tell the
9280               	; 	' two apart is the fault that once deleted the second floor's support.
9281               	; 	#if NES
9282               	; 	#nbc = #bca - 8288
9283               	; 	#nbc = #nbc + 32

10202               	;
10203               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
10204               	; 	'
10205               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
10206               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
10207               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
10208               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
10209               	; 	'
10210               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
10211               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
10212               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
10213               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10214               	; 	'
10215               	; 	' TWO DRAINS CAP THE STEP AT 2 PER FRAME whatever psp64 says (CLAUDE.md
10216               	; 	' 3A: N drains cap the speed at N, and the surplus leaks into a byte that
10217               	; 	' wraps). Every caller is under that: Kelly 102/64 = 1.6, the fastest
10218               	; 	' hazard 76/64 = 1.2, Harry 57/64 = 0.9, the bounce phase 25/64 = 0.4.
10219               	; 	'
10220               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
10221               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
10222               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
10223               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
10224               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
10225               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.

10714               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10715               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10716               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10717               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10718               	; 	' runs every pass.
10719               	; 	'
10720               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10721               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10722               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10723               	; 	'
10724               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10725               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10726               	; 	'
10727               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10728               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10729               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10730               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10731               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10732               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10733               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10734               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10735               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10736               	; 	'
10737               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
10738               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
10739               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10740               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10741               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10742               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no
10743               	; 	' chase at all. checkchase.py holds the line.
10744               	; 	' STILL RUNNING FROM THE STAIRS -- and this has to come BEFORE the move,
10745               	; 	' not after it. It sat below the two `IF hmv` blocks, where all it could
10746               	; 	' still reach was the animation counter: he faced the right way, played
10747               	; 	' the run cycle and did not travel a pixel. He stood at the foot of the
10748               	; 	' flight looking busy.

10750               	; 	' TWO THINGS END THE RUN, AND BOTH ARE VISIBLE ON SCREEN.

10845               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10846               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10847               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10848               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10849               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10850               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10851               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10852               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10853               	; 	'
10854               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10855               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10856               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10857               	; 	'
10858               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10859               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10860               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10861               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10862               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10863               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10864               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10865               	; 	'
10866               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10867               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10868               	; 	'
10869               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10870               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10871               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10872               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10873               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10874               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10875               	; 	'
10876               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10877               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10878               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
10879               	; 	' before any of this.
10880               	; 	'
10881               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
10882               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10883               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the
10884               	; 	' steps run backwards (CLAUDE.md 3A, DESIGN.md 0f). It is about 3% of his
10885               	; 	' journey.
10886               	; 	'
10887               	; 	' `hanim` still advances by hspd and is still an ODOMETER -- pixels
10888               	; 	' travelled, not time -- so the run cycle stays locked to the ground at any

11350               	;
11351               	; 	' ======================================================================
11352               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11353               	; 	' ======================================================================
11354               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11355               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11356               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11357               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11358               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11359               	; 	'
11360               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11361               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11362               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11363               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11364               	; 	' broken.
11365               	; 	'
11366               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11367               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11368               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11369               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11370               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11371               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11372               	; 	'
11373               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11374               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11375               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11376               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.

11933               	; 	' AND THEY HAVE TO BE AT THE SAME HEIGHT, NOT MERELY ON THE SAME FLOOR.
11934               	; 	'
11935               	; 	' `hlv` does not change until a ride ENDS -- a crook stepping onto a
11936               	; 	' flight keeps the floor he left until he arrives at the next one. So
11937               	; 	' while he was most of a storey up or down the stairs he still counted as
11938               	; 	' standing on the floor he started from, and a Kop who ran over the head
11939               	; 	' of the flight arrested him through the floor. Reported from play:
11940               	; 	' "I run over top of him, even though we do not touch".
11941               	; 	'
11942               	; 	' It is the same shape of bug as the catch that fired at MAXIMUM
11943               	; 	' separation: a test that is right about one axis and silent about the
11944               	; 	' other, where the silent one happens to be true nearly all the time.
11945               	; 	'

11947               	; 	' below it, which is a signed quantity, and CVBasic's variables are not.

11949               	; 	' climb plus Harry's descent on one side, Harry's climb on the other --
11950               	; 	' and the difference is taken between two numbers that cannot go
11951               	; 	' negative. Two riders passing on the same flight measure the sum of

12058               	; 	' RIDING WITH THE DOORS SHUT: HIDE HIM AND DO NOT DRAW HIM AT ALL.
12059               	; 	'
12060               	; 	' This test used to sit AFTER his sprites had been written, so every pass
12061               	; 	' placed him at his old floor and then hid him again. That is not free.
12062               	; 	' CVBasic's SPRITE writes a RAM mirror which the vblank ISR copies to
12063               	; 	' VRAM, so a vblank landing BETWEEN the draw and the hide latches the
12064               	; 	' visible state for a frame -- and draw_actors is long (Kelly, Harry,
12065               	; 	' eight obstacles) while a pass on the lift screen spans two or three
12066               	; 	' frames, so it happened constantly. He flickered at the floor he had
12067               	; 	' just left, which reads as a drawing bug rather than as a journey.
12068               	; 	'
12069               	; 	' Deciding BEFORE drawing costs one test and cannot race the ISR at all:
12070               	; 	' the mirror never holds a position to be caught with.
12071               	; 	IF klst = ST_ELEV THEN
12072 E42A D020  34 	movb @cvb_KLST,r0
     E42C 21C0

12281               	; 		' FOUR RUN FRAMES FROM TWO BITS of the animation counter, and no
12282               	; 		' divide -- `/` compiles to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and
12283               	; 		' this is per-frame code. Two adjacent bits give 0,4,8,12.

12285               	; 		' KELLY USES BITS 2 AND 3 AND HARRY USES 3 AND 4, because a stride

12636               	; 	' and lowest at contact; with the body pinned at a constant y, alternating
12637               	; 	' legs under a motionless torso reads as a dance rather than as travel.
12638               	; 	'

12640               	; 	' keep their y, so the planted foot stays on the floor and the figure
12641               	; 	' stretches at the waist instead of hopping. Lifting the legs too would be
12642               	; 	' a jump.

12645               	; 	' cycle's LOW beat bit. IT MUST MOVE WITH THE BEAT BITS ABOVE IT: on the
12646               	; 	' wrong bit he rises and falls twice per stride, a second clock inside one
12647               	; 	' figure, which is the flapping of DESIGN.md 0j2 in the vertical.
12648               	; 	'

12650               	; 	' `same level AND |dx| < CATCHR`. Doing this to Kelly would desynchronise

13123               	; 	' THE SCANNER
13124               	; 	' ======================================================================
13125               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
13126               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table
13127               	; 	' traffic. With the flip (DESIGN.md 2a) this is how you know where Harry
13128               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
13129               	; 	'
13130               	; 	' Rows 21-23 all sit in the THIRD screen third, so every scanner pattern
13131               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
13132               	; 	'
13133               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
13134               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
13135               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
13136               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
13137               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
13138               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
13139               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
13140               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
13141               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
13142               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so
13143               	; 	' the steps travel up the flight rather than drifting sideways.

13169               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
13170               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
13171               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
13172               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
13173               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
13174               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
13175               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
13176               	; 	'
13177               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
13178               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
13179               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
13180               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
13181               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
13182               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
13183               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.
13184               	; 	escp = escp + 1

13197               	; 	#if NES
13198               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
13199               	; 	'
13200               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
13201               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
13202               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
13203               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
13204               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
13205               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
13206               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
13207               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
13208               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
13209               	; 	'
13210               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
13211               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
13212               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
13213               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
13214               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
13215               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13216               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13217               	; 	'
13218               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13219               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13220               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13221               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13222               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13223               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13224               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13225               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13226               	; 	' with room to spare.
13227               	; 	'
13228               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13229               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13230               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13231               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13232               	; 	WAIT
13233               	; 	#endif
13234               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
13235               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13236               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13237               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13238               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13239               	; 	'
13240               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13241               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13242               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13243               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
13244               	; 	'
13245               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
13246               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the
13247               	; 	' roof, so it needed both composite sets -- nine characters against the
13248               	; 	' east's six, 216 bytes a pass against 144. It measured 20 passes a
13249               	; 	' second where the east screen managed 24-26. The two sets are
13250               	; 	' PIXEL-IDENTICAL and are never wanted in the same screen THIRD, so they
13251               	; 	' share their characters now and are told apart by the per-third colour
13252               	; 	' table (see esc_deck_col in setup). Six either side.
13253               	; 	'
13254               	; 	' The handrail and the frame sit past the end of both ranges and never

13552               	;
13553               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------- the scanner's furniture
13554               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is
13555               	; 	' somewhere, but not what he is near, which is the one thing you actually
13556               	; 	' need when he is off-screen. Floor lines say which level, the slashes say
13557               	; 	' where that floor's escalator is, and the bar says where the elevator is --
13558               	; 	' exactly the three things the manual lists.
13559               	; 	'
13560               	; 	' FURNITURE AND DOTS ARE SEGREGATED BY PIXEL ROW ON PURPOSE, and a level
13561               	; 	' band is now FOUR rows, one per colour, because a pixel row carries
13562               	; 	' exactly one colour here:
13563               	; 	'
13564               	; 	'   +0  GREY    escalator head, and the elevator car
13565               	; 	'   +1  GREY    the air of that floor
13566               	; 	'   +2  GREY
13567               	; 	'   +3  YELLOW  the floor line -- and NOTHING else goes here
13568               	; 	'
13569               	; 	' THE FIRST THREE ROWS ARE THE FLOOR'S AIR AND EVERYTHING LIVES IN THEM:
13570               	; 	' the escalator's three-step diagonal, the lift car, and both actors, all
13571               	; 	' three pixels tall. They are grey in the table, and the Kop and the
13572               	; 	' crook recolour their own CHARACTER as they move (scan_mark) -- which is
13573               	; 	' what lets both of them fill the band instead of getting a pixel row
13574               	; 	' each. Eight pixels of this canvas is half a screen of the store, so
13575               	; 	' they are almost never in one character; when they are, they merge.
13576               	; 	'
13577               	; 	' Shrinking from six rows bought eight empty pixel rows, four above the
13578               	; 	' instrument and four below, so it no longer butts against the shop floor
13579               	; 	' above it or the bottom of the screen.
13580               	; 	'
13581               	; 	' The dots are erased by ANDing their bits out, so anything sharing a row
13582               	; 	' with one is rubbed away wherever an actor has passed -- which is why
13583               	; 	' scan_escs and scan_elev redraw every tick rather than once.

13855               	; 	' THE ONE READ-MODIFY-WRITE ON THE PATTERN TABLE. The radar ORs a
13856               	; 	' pixel row into a canvas character, so it has to know what is already

13858               	; 	' and which only this routine writes -- so it is exact, not an

13970               	;
13971               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
13972               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
13973               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
13974               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
13975               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
13976               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
13977               	; scan_wipe:
13978               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
13979               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
13980               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
13981               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
13982               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
13983               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
13984               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
13985               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
13986               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
13987               	; 	'
13988               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
13989               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
13990               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
13991               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
13992               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
13993               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
13994               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
13995               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
13996               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
13997               	; 	'
13998               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
13999               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
14000               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
14001               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
14002               	; 	'
14003               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
14004               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.

14008               	; 	#if NES
14009               	; 	' AN NES TILE IS SIXTEEN BYTES, NOT EIGHT -- two bitplanes. DERIVED FROM
14010               	; 	' THE LINE ABOVE rather than written out again: renumber.py rewrites that
14011               	; 	' literal out of genart.SCAN_FIRST and checkstruct.py checks it, and a

14029               	; 	' by the same offset the PPU address uses, so it grows with the stride --
14030               	; 	' half of what it holds is the second bitplane, which this port never sets
14031               	; 	' and scan_or1 therefore never reads as ink.
14032               	; 	' AND THE CANVAS IS WIPED TO GREEN, NOT TO BLACK.
14033               	; 	'
14034               	; 	' On the TI a blank canvas is zeros and the COLOUR TABLE says what the
14035               	; 	' background is. There is no colour table here: a pixel's colour is its
14036               	; 	' two bitplane bits, so "green background" means plane 0 SET everywhere
14037               	; 	' and plane 1 clear -- index 1, which is the store's green in P0.
14038               	; 	'
14039               	; 	' THAT INVERTS THE SENSE OF EVERY FEATURE DRAWN ON TOP. The floor lines
14040               	; 	' add plane 1 to reach index 3 (gold), and the escalator diagonals CLEAR
14041               	; 	' plane 0 to reach index 0 (the backdrop, black) -- see scan_or1, which
14042               	; 	' is why it ANDs here and ORs on the TI. Writing zeros here instead would
14043               	; 	' leave the instrument black-on-black and the flights invisible.
14044               	; 	'
14045               	; 	' A tile is sixteen bytes: 0-7 are plane 0 and 8-15 plane 1, so the byte's
14046               	; 	' position within its tile decides which it is.
14047               	; 	' AND THE MARGINS ARE GREY, WHICH IS THE OTHER BITPLANE PAIR.
14048               	; 	'
14049               	; 	' The canvas is three character rows -- 24 pixel rows -- of which the
14050               	; 	' instrument uses the middle SIXTEEN (rows 4-19: four levels of four).
14051               	; 	' The outer eight are deliberate air, four above and four below, so the
14052               	; 	' radar does not butt against the shop floor above it or the screen edge
14053               	; 	' below. On the TI those rows take the scanner's own background; here they
14054               	; 	' are index 2, the store's grey, against the instrument's green.
14055               	; 	'
14056               	; 	' Two bitplanes give the four colours this canvas needs and nothing else
14057               	; 	' has to change: index 1 green is plane 0, index 2 grey is plane 1, and
14058               	; 	' the floor lines and flights work on top of those (scan_furn, scan_or1).
14059               	; 	'
14060               	; 	' The byte's place in the canvas says which it is. 256 bytes is one
14061               	; 	' CHARACTER row (16 tiles of 16), the low three bits are the pixel row
14062               	; 	' within the tile, and bit 3 of the position picks the bitplane.

14587               	;
14588               	; #if NES
14589               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
14590               	; 	' THE ATTRIBUTE TABLE -- the NES's only way of giving two parts of the
14591               	; 	' screen different colours.
14592               	; 	'
14593               	; 	' 64 bytes at $23C0. Each byte covers FOUR character rows and four
14594               	; 	' columns, split into four 2x2 quadrants of two bits each: bits 0-1 top
14595               	; 	' left, 2-3 top right, 4-5 bottom left, 6-7 bottom right.
14596               	; 	'
14597               	; 	' The picture sits three rows down for overscan, which lands the regions
14598               	; 	' on block boundaries almost by luck:
14599               	; 	'
14600               	; 	'   byte row 0   name rows 0-3    the HUD is row 3  -> bottom quads P1
14601               	; 	'   byte row 1   name rows 4-7    the sky, top half -> P2, bottom -> P3
14602               	; 	'   byte rows 2+ name rows 8-29   the store         -> P0
14603               	; 	'
14604               	; 	' $50 is "bottom two quadrants on palette 1"; $FA is "top two on palette
14605               	; 	' 2, bottom two on palette 3", which is what splits the sunset into a
14606               	; 	' blue band over a warm one. Written as bare literals because this is the
14607               	; 	' one place the bit layout is visible, and naming them would hide it.
14608               	; 	'
14609               	; 	' 64 VPOKEs is 192 bytes of PPU queue, and WRTVRM waits when the 64-byte
14610               	; 	' buffer fills, so this paces itself across three frames and cannot
14611               	; 	' overrun vblank the way a single big SCREEN blit can.
14612               	; nes_attr:
14613               	; 	#nav = 9152			' $23C0
14614               	; 	' $55, NOT $50 -- ALL FOUR QUADRANTS ON P1, not just the bottom two.
14615               	; 	'
14616               	; 	' $50 put the HUD's own row (name row 2) on P1 and left rows 0-1 on P0.
14617               	; 	' That was invisible while text sat on the backdrop, and stopped being so
14618               	; 	' the moment the font gained a PAPER: rows 0-1 are blank cells, and a blank
14619               	; 	' cell is all paper, so they came out in P0's index 1 -- the store's GREEN
14620               	; 	' -- as a green band above the score line. Nothing is drawn up there, so
14621               	; 	' putting the whole byte on P1 costs nothing and the HUD reads as one band
14622               	; 	' of dark blue running into the sky.
14623               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 7
14624               	; 		VPOKE #nav,85
14625               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14626               	; 	NEXT nai
14627               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 7
14628               	; 		VPOKE #nav,170			' $AA -- the whole sky band on P2, no second palette
14629               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14630               	; 	NEXT nai
14631               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 47
14632               	; 		VPOKE #nav,0
14633               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14634               	; 	NEXT nai
14635               	; 	RETURN
14636               	; #endif
14637               	;

14639               	; 	' DIV on this CPU, and only run when the value actually changes.

15082               	;
15083               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15084               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15085               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15086               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15087               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15088               	; 	'
15089               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15090               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15091               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15092               	; 	'
15093               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15094               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15095               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15096               	; 	'
15097               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15098               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15099               	; 	'
15100               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15101               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15102               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15103               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15104               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15105               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15106               	; 	'
15107               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15108               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15109               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15110               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15111               	; 	'
15112               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15113               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15114               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
15115               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)

15232               	;
15233               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
15234               	; 	'
15235               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15236               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15237               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15238               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15239               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15240               	; 	'
15241               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15242               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15243               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15244               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15245               	; 	' counting stops.
15246               	;
15247               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
15248               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15249               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15250               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15251               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15252               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15253               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15254               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
15255               	; 	'
15256               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
15257               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
15258               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).
15259               	;

15297               	; 	' AND THE SAME BEFORE THE MESSAGE BOX. Losing on the clock means the
15298               	; 	' flash was running, so without this the last thing the player sees is
15299               	; 	' whichever half of the field the final pass happened to leave behind.

     F842 A980     
15302 F844 F66A     	data cvb_TIME_SHOW
15303               	; 	' THE CAST IS NOT TAKEN AWAY YET -- hide_all now runs AFTER the beat.
15304               	; 	'
15305               	; 	' It used to run here, so the moment the clock emptied, Harry and the
15306               	; 	' thing that had just hit him vanished and the sound played over an empty
15307               	; 	' store. The hit that ENDS a round is the worst case: `do_hit` sets tout
15308               	; 	' before the freeze starts and the main loop leaves on the very next pass,
15309               	; 	' so the hit sound gets one tick and everything is already gone.
15310               	; 	'
15311               	; 	' The pause drains the sound; leaving the actors up means it drains over
15312               	; 	' the picture that caused it. Nothing is moving -- the pause ticks sfx_tick
15313               	; 	' and nothing else -- so it is a held tableau, not a frozen game.
15314               	; 	' THE MESSAGE BOX, ON THE GAME SCREEN AND NOT INSTEAD OF IT.
15315               	; 	'
15316               	; 	' It used to CLS before GAME OVER, so the last thing the player saw was
15317               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which
15318               	; 	' reads as the program ending rather than as the game ending. The store
15319               	; 	' stays; the message sits in the middle of it.
15320               	; 	'
15321               	; 	' THE BOX IS THE FONT'S OWN BACKGROUND. Every font character is black on
15322               	; 	' HUD_BG (dark blue), so a row of SPACES is a solid dark blue bar. A blank
15323               	; 	' row above and below the text is a frame for the price of two strings and
15324               	; 	' no new characters, and it reads against the store because nothing else on
15325               	; 	' the playfield is that colour.
15326               	; 	'
15327               	; 	' THIRTEEN WIDE, WHICH IS THE LONGEST MESSAGE PLUS ONE EITHER SIDE.
15328               	; 	' HE GOT AWAY and THE BIPLANE are both eleven. Every string below is padded
15329               	; 	' to exactly thirteen so the box has straight edges, and column 10 puts it
15330               	; 	' at columns 10-22 -- centre 16, the screen's.
15331               	; 	'
15332               	; 	' THE REASON IS ALWAYS ON THE SAME ROW, and that is what lets one layout

15558               	;
15559               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15560               	; 	'
15561               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15562               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15563               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15564               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15565               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15566               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15567               	; 	'
15568               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15569               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15570               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
15571               	; 	'
15572               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
15573               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
15574               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
15575               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
15576               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
15577               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
15578               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
15579               	; 	'
15580               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
15581               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
15582               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
15583               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
15584               	; 	'
15585               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
15586               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
15587               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
15588               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
15589               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
15590               	; 	'
15591               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
15592               	; 	' did not finish.

15956               	;
15957               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
15958               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
15959               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
15960               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
15961               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
15962               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
15963               	;
15964               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
15965               	; 	'
15966               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
15967               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
15968               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
15969               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
15970               	; 	'
15971               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
15972               	; 	'
15973               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
15974               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
15975               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
15976               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
15977               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
15978               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
15979               	; 	'
15980               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
15981               	; 	'
15982               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
15983               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
15984               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
15985               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
15986               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
15987               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
15988               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
15989               	; 	'
15990               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
15991               	; 	'
15992               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
15993               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
15994               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
15995               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
15996               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
15997               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
15998               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
15999               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16000               	; 	'
16001               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16002               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16003               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16004               	; 	'
16005               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16006               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16007               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16008               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16009               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16010               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16011               	; 	'
16012               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16013               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
16014               	; 	'
16015               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
16016               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
16017               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
16018               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
16019               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
16020               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
16021               	; 	'
16022               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
16023               	; 	'
16024               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
16025               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
16026               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to

16229               	;
16230               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16231               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16232               	; 	'
16233               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16234               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16235               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16236               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16237               	; 	'
16238               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16239               	; 	'
16240               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16241               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16242               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16243               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16244               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16245               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16246               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16247               	; 	'
16248               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16249               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16250               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16251               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16252               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16253               	; 	'
16254               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16255               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16256               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16257               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16258               	; 	#if TI994A
16259               	; 	BANK 2
16260      01EC     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$
